title: How to Read Drone Law: Rules Change, Always Verify the Source
html:
This part is a map, not the territory

Drone regulation is one of the fastest-moving areas of aviation law. The rules described in this part reflect the US framework as of the time of writing, but registration thresholds, Remote ID enforcement dates, recreational test details, and import policy can and do change. Treat every number and procedure here as a starting point you will re-verify against the primary source before you fly. This lesson teaches you the durable skill that outlasts any specific rule: how to find and trust authoritative sources.

Who actually makes the rules (US)

  • FAA (Federal Aviation Administration) — the national authority for the airspace. Federal rules preempt the airspace itself: altitude, airspace authorizations, registration, Remote ID, and operating rules (recreational Exception vs Part 107) all come from the FAA.
  • Congress / NDAA — statutes (laws passed by Congress) that direct the FAA and shape things like the recreational Exception and the foreign-drone debate covered in Lesson 8.
  • State & local government — cannot regulate the airspace, but can regulate takeoff/landing, trespass, privacy, harassment, and park use. A city can ban launching from a public park even where the FAA allows the flight.
  • Land managers — the National Park Service, US Forest Service, BLM, and private landowners set their own surface rules.
Layered rules.
A flight can be perfectly legal under the FAA and still illegal under a city ordinance or park rule. You must clear every layer, not just the federal one.

What counts as an authoritative source

Rank your sources. Primary government pages beat forums, YouTube, and even this course.

SourceTrustUse for
faa.gov/uasPrimaryRegistration, Part 107, Remote ID, recreational rules
FAA B4UFLY / Aloft / approved LAANC appsPrimary dataAirspace, LAANC authorizations
tfr.faa.govPrimaryTemporary Flight Restrictions
Federal Register / eCFR (14 CFR Part 107)Primary (legal text)Exact regulatory wording
Manufacturer docs (DJI, etc.)SecondaryWhether your model has built-in Remote ID
Forums, YouTube, this courseTertiaryOrientation only — always confirm
Safety mindset.
The same discipline applies to flight safety. Before every session you will repeat a verification ritual: current TFRs, battery condition, firmware, and a props-off arm test. Legal compliance and physical safety are the same habit — check the source, every time.

Flying abroad or out of state

The moment you cross a national border, the FAA framework stops applying. The EU uses EASA categories (Open/Specific/Certified) with their own class marks and operator IDs; the UK CAA, Transport Canada, and CASA in Australia each differ again. Never assume your US registration or TRUST certificate carries over. Search the destination country's civil aviation authority before you pack the drone.

verification log (example)
# keep this with your gear, update before each trip FAA UAS rules ........ verified 2026-06-01 (faa.gov/uas) Remote ID status ..... verified 2026-06-01 Local park rules ..... verified 2026-05-20 (city.gov) NEXT RE-CHECK ........ before next flight day
▸Hands-On

Build your authoritative-source bookmark set and a verification log.

  1. Bookmark faa.gov/uas, tfr.faa.gov, and your LAANC app of choice.
  2. If you fly outside the US, bookmark that country's civil aviation authority page too.
  3. Create a verification log (paper card or note) listing each source and the date you last checked it.
  4. Write a personal rule: "I re-verify TFRs and airspace before every flight day."

title: FAA Registration: Who Must Register & How
html:
The weight threshold

In the US, the dividing line for registration is 0.55 lb (250 g). If your aircraft weighs more than 250 g at takeoff (including battery, props, and any payload like a camera or cargo), you must register it with the FAA before you fly outdoors. Sub-250 g drones flown recreationally are exempt from registration — which is exactly why the DJI Mini line is built to land just under 250 g. Note the asymmetry: if you fly any drone commercially under Part 107, it must be registered regardless of weight.

Your droneUseRegister?
Under 250 gRecreationalNo
Under 250 gPart 107 / commercialYes
250 g and overAnyYes
Weigh it for real.
Don't trust the spec sheet. A Mini with ND filters, a prop guard, or a heavier aftermarket battery can cross 250 g. Put it on a kitchen scale, fully assembled, ready to fly.

Two registration tracks

  • Recreational (Exception for Limited Recreational Operations) — one registration number covers all the drones you fly for fun. Cost is a small fee (historically $5), valid 3 years. You must be 13 or older to register; under 13 needs an adult to register for them.
  • Part 107 — each aircraft is registered individually and gets its own number. Same fee per aircraft, 3-year validity.

Both are done at the FAA's DroneZone portal (faadronezone.faa.gov). You'll create an account, choose the correct track (recreational vs Part 107 — they are separate dashboards), enter the drone make/model and serial, pay, and receive a registration certificate as a PDF.

Marking the aircraft

Required marking.
Your registration number must be legible and on the exterior of the aircraft. Since a 2019 rule, it can no longer be hidden in a battery compartment — the number must be visible without tools so first responders can read it. A label on the underside of the body shell is standard.

Use a label maker or a fine paint pen. Cover it with clear tape so it survives crashes and rain. Carry proof of registration (the PDF on your phone is fine) whenever you fly; an FAA inspector or law enforcement officer can ask for it.

DroneZone flow
1. Create account at faadronezone.faa.gov 2. Choose dashboard: Recreational Flyers -> one number, all drones Part 107 -> register each aircraft 3. Enter make / model / serial 4. Pay fee (~$5), valid 3 years 5. Download certificate PDF 6. Label exterior with the number, cover with clear tape
Pre-flight safety, not just paperwork.
Registration proves the drone is yours; it does nothing for safety. Pair it with a physical check: props seated and undamaged, battery not puffed, firmware current. A loose prop or a swollen LiPo will ruin your day far faster than a missing label.
▸Hands-On

Register your aircraft (or walk the full DroneZone flow) and mark it.

  1. Weigh your drone ready-to-fly on a kitchen scale; record grams.
  2. If 250 g+ (or any Part 107 use), create a DroneZone account and complete registration.
  3. Download the certificate PDF to your phone.
  4. Label the exterior with your number and seal it with clear tape; photograph the placement.

title: Recreational (TRUST) vs Commercial (Part 107)
html:
The one question that decides your path

The FAA does not care how much fun you're having — it cares about purpose. Ask: does this flight produce anything of value to anyone, including me? If the answer is no — you fly purely for personal enjoyment and the footage stays a personal memory — you may operate under the Exception for Limited Recreational Operations. The moment the flight serves a business purpose, you need a Part 107 Remote Pilot Certificate.

Commercial is broader than you think.
Posting footage to a monetized YouTube channel, shooting a friend's wedding "for free" as a favor that builds your portfolio, inspecting your own rental property, or mapping a field for your farm — all of these have been treated as non-recreational. When in doubt, get Part 107. It is the safer default.

The recreational path: TRUST

Recreational flyers must pass TRUST (The Recreational UAS Safety Test). It is free, taken online through an FAA-approved test administrator, has no expiration, and cannot be failed in a meaningful sense — you cannot move past a question until you answer it correctly, so everyone who finishes passes. It takes about 30 minutes and covers basic airspace, where you can fly, and safety.

  • You receive a completion certificate (PDF). Save it — there is no central lookup. If you lose it, you retake the test.
  • Carry it (phone is fine) when flying recreationally.
  • Recreational flyers must also follow the FAA's recreational rules and fly within the safety guidelines of a recognized community-based organization (CBO).

The commercial path: Part 107

Part 107 is a real FAA airman certificate. You must be 16+, pass a TSA security screening, and pass the Aeronautical Knowledge Test — a ~60-question proctored exam at an FAA testing center covering airspace, weather, sectional charts, loading, and regulations. You need ~70% to pass. The certificate requires a recurrent (free online) training every 24 months to stay current.

TRUST (Recreational)Part 107 (Commercial)
CostFree~$175 exam fee
WhereOnline, self-pacedProctored testing center
AgeNone to take (13+ to register drone)16+
RenewalNever expiresRecurrent every 24 months
Lets youFly for fun onlyFly for any purpose, incl. business
Waivers (e.g. night, BVLOS)NoYes, via FAA waiver
Part 107 unlocks more.
Beyond legality, Part 107 lets you request waivers for operations recreational flyers can't do, and it's table stakes for insurance and client work. Many serious hobbyists get it just for the airspace knowledge.
Certificate is not competence.
Passing a test does not make you safe. Keep your props-off habits, your battery discipline, and your VLOS rules no matter which path you're on. The FAA can revoke either credential for reckless operation.
▸Hands-On

Take TRUST and decide whether you actually need Part 107.

  1. Find an FAA-approved TRUST administrator and complete the free test.
  2. Download and save the completion certificate to your phone and a backup.
  3. Write down your intended uses (YouTube? client photos? just fun?).
  4. For each use, decide: recreational or commercial? If any is commercial, note that Part 107 is required.

title: Remote ID: Broadcast vs Module
html:
What Remote ID is

Remote ID (RID) is a "digital license plate" for drones. While flying, your aircraft continuously broadcasts — over Wi-Fi/Bluetooth, locally, not over the internet — a message anyone with a compatible receiver app can pick up. It is the FAA's foundation for safely integrating drones into the airspace and for accountability (law enforcement can identify an aircraft near an airport or a crowd).

The broadcast message includes, roughly: a unique ID for the aircraft, its current position and altitude, its velocity, the position of the control station (the pilot's takeoff point), an emergency status, and a timestamp. It does not publish your name or address — those stay in the FAA registration database, not in the air.

Who must comply.
Generally, any drone that requires registration must also meet Remote ID when operated. Sub-250 g recreational drones that don't require registration are exempt from RID. As always, confirm current applicability on faa.gov — enforcement dates and thresholds have shifted before.

Three ways to comply

  1. Standard Remote ID (built-in broadcast) — the drone has RID baked into the firmware/hardware and broadcasts the full message set including takeoff location. Most current DJI, Autel, and Skydio consumer drones ship this way. Check the manufacturer's compliance list and keep firmware current.
  2. Remote ID Broadcast Module (add-on) — a small self-contained device with its own battery and GPS that you attach to an older or self-built drone. It broadcasts the aircraft ID, the module's position, and the takeoff location (the point where the module first got a GPS lock). It does not report the control-station location, which is the main difference from standard RID.
  3. FRIA (FAA-Recognized Identification Area) — a specific approved site (often a club flying field) where you may legally fly drones without RID. This is the path for hobbyists building or flying legacy/RID-incapable aircraft.
Standard RID (built-in)Broadcast Module
Who it's forModern factory dronesOlder / DIY / non-RID drones
Reports control-station location?YesNo (reports takeoff point)
PowerFrom aircraftOwn small battery
Fly outside its limits?Anywhere allowedVLOS only (no FPV beyond sight)

Modules: mounting and gotchas

A broadcast module (e.g. units from BlueMark such as the DroneBeacon, or Dronetag) typically attaches with adhesive or a strap and adds 10-30 g. On a tight quad that weight matters — and crossing 250 g may itself trigger registration. The module must have its own clear sky view for GPS, must be powered on for the whole flight, and you must include its serial in your FAA registration (DroneZone has a field for the RID serial number).

Don't let RID compromise the airframe.
Mount the module so it can't shift into a prop arc or block cooling vents. Re-balance after adding it. Confirm GPS lock and broadcast before arming — a module with a dead battery is non-compliant and you won't know mid-flight.
▸Hands-On

Determine your Remote ID compliance and plan a fix if needed.

  1. Look up your exact drone model on the FAA's Remote ID declaration list to see if it has standard built-in RID.
  2. Update firmware; confirm the manual states RID is active.
  3. If non-compliant, identify a specific broadcast module that fits, note its weight, and describe how/where it attaches with GPS sky view.
  4. Add the module's serial to your DroneZone registration record.

title: Airspace Classes & LAANC Authorizations
html:
Controlled vs uncontrolled — the core idea

US airspace is divided into classes. For drone pilots the practical split is simple: controlled airspace (where air traffic control manages traffic, usually around airports) requires authorization before you fly; uncontrolled airspace (Class G) generally does not. Most rural and suburban ground is Class G to 400 ft and you can fly recreationally or under Part 107 without asking — but you still owe TFRs, VLOS, and altitude limits.

ClassWhereDrone authorization?
GUncontrolled (rural, away from airports)None needed (still follow all rules)
E (surface)Some airport areas down to groundAuthorization required
DSmaller towered airportsAuthorization required
CBusier airportsAuthorization required
BMajor metro airports (e.g. LAX, ATL)Authorization required
Hard rule.
Never fly in controlled airspace without authorization. Doing so near an airport endangers crewed aircraft and is one of the most serious violations the FAA pursues. "I didn't know it was Class D" is not a defense — checking is free and takes seconds.

LAANC: how authorization actually works

LAANC (Low Altitude Authorization and Notification Capability, say "lance") is the automated system that grants near-instant approval to fly in controlled airspace. The FAA publishes UAS Facility Maps that pre-define a maximum altitude for each grid cell around an airport — often 0, 50, 100, 200, 300, or 400 ft AGL depending on how close you are to the runway. If your requested altitude is at or below the grid ceiling, LAANC approves it instantly through an approved app; if you need higher, you submit a further coordination request that a human at the FAA reviews (days, not seconds).

  • Approved apps include Aloft (formerly Airmap), Avision, and others; the FAA also runs B4UFLY for situational awareness (B4UFLY shows you the airspace but you authorize through a LAANC provider).
  • Both recreational flyers and Part 107 pilots can use LAANC.
  • An authorization is tied to a specific area, altitude ceiling, and time window. Fly within it.
reading a UAS facility grid cell
Cell ceiling: 100 ft AGL You request: 90 ft, 2pm-4pm today -> LAANC auto-approves in seconds You request: 250 ft -> exceeds grid -> further coordination (manual, slow) Cell ceiling: 0 ft (runway approach) -> no auto authorization here at all
AGL, not MSL.
The 400 ft limit and grid ceilings are above ground level at your launch point, not altitude above sea level. The drone's reported altitude in your app is what you watch.
Authorization is not a safety pass.
LAANC clears the paperwork, not the sky. Keep your eyes up, watch for crewed aircraft and other drones, and yield to everything. If you hear or see a helicopter or low aircraft, descend and land immediately regardless of your authorization.
▸Hands-On

Check a real spot and request (or simulate) a LAANC authorization.

  1. Install a LAANC app (Aloft) and B4UFLY.
  2. Drop a pin on a place you actually want to fly; read the airspace class and grid ceiling.
  3. If it's controlled, set an altitude at or below the ceiling and a time window, then request authorization.
  4. Screenshot the result (class, ceiling, approval status) and save it with your flight notes.

title: No-Fly Zones: Airports, TFRs, Restricted Areas & National Parks
html:
Categories of "no"

Beyond airspace class, several distinct prohibitions can ground you even in otherwise-open Class G. Learn the categories so you recognize each one on the map.

  • Airport surface areas — covered by LAANC in controlled airspace (Lesson 5). Around some small uncontrolled airports you should still stay clear of approach/departure paths and give way to all crewed traffic.
  • Temporary Flight Restrictions (TFRs) — short-lived no-fly bubbles. They pop up for wildfires, major sporting events (stadiums get a standing 3-nautical-mile TFR from 1 hour before to 1 hour after games over a certain capacity), VIP/presidential movement, disaster areas, and security events. A presidential TFR can blanket a large area for days with no warning.
  • Prohibited & Restricted Areas (P/R) — permanent special-use airspace over sensitive sites: military ranges, the White House and DC, nuclear facilities, certain federal sites. "Prohibited" (P-) means never; "Restricted" (R-) means only when not active.
  • National Parks — the National Park Service bans launching, landing, or operating drones from within virtually all NPS-managed land. You also can't fly over a park if you launched outside to skirt the rule. National Forests (USFS) and BLM land are often more permissive but have their own rules and wilderness-area exceptions.
  • Critical infrastructure & local bans — power plants, prisons, military bases (Section 130i no-drone zones), stadiums, and many cities/parks have their own surface restrictions.
Check TFRs EVERY flight day.
This is the one that catches good pilots. A wildfire TFR or a presidential visit can appear overnight over a spot you've flown safely a hundred times. Flying into a wildfire TFR can ground firefighting aircraft and kill people on the ground; the FAA and DOJ prosecute it aggressively. Check tfr.faa.gov or your LAANC app the morning of every flight.

How to actually check

pre-flight no-fly check
[ ] Airspace class at pin .... LAANC app [ ] Active TFRs today ........ tfr.faa.gov / app (re-check day-of) [ ] Prohibited/Restricted .... sectional / app overlay [ ] Land manager ............. NPS=NO, city park ordinance? [ ] Stadium event nearby? .... 3 NM TFR window [ ] Critical infra / 130i .... no-drone zone overlay All clear -> plan flight Any flag -> relocate
Two-map habit.
No single app catches everything. Cross-check a LAANC/airspace app (class, grids, RTFR) and the land owner/manager rules (NPS, city ordinance, private property). Federal clearance does not grant you permission to launch from someone else's ground.
Stadium gotcha.
The standing sports-stadium TFR (MLB, NFL, NCAA D-I, NASCAR over the capacity threshold) extends to 3 nautical miles and 3,000 ft, active around game time. People launch from a "safe" park nearby and don't realize a stadium two miles away just put them in a federal violation.
▸Hands-On

Map the prohibitions around where you live.

  1. Open tfr.faa.gov and your LAANC app; list any active TFRs in your region today.
  2. Identify any Prohibited/Restricted areas within ~25 miles.
  3. List five specific nearby places you cannot fly and the reason for each (NPS, stadium TFR, restricted area, city park ban, airport surface).
  4. Add the "check TFRs every flight day" line to your pre-flight checklist.

title: Altitude & VLOS Limits, Privacy & Courtesy
html:
The core operating limits

Two numbers and one principle define safe, legal flying in the US for both recreational and Part 107 operations (absent a waiver):

  • 400 ft AGL maximum altitude. Above ground level at your location. The exception: under Part 107 you may fly higher than 400 ft if you stay within 400 ft of a structure (e.g. inspecting a 600 ft tower), which keeps you clear of crewed traffic that flies the open sky above 500 ft.
  • Visual Line of Sight (VLOS). You (or a visual observer in direct communication with you) must keep the aircraft in unaided sight at all times — naked eye, glasses or contacts are fine, but binoculars and the FPV goggle feed are not. You must be able to see the drone's orientation and the airspace around it to see-and-avoid.
  • Daylight and twilight with anti-collision lighting visible for 3 statute miles for night flight (recreational night flying requires the lighting too).
FPV and VLOS.
First-person-view flying does not satisfy VLOS by itself — the goggles are an aid, not your eyes. The standard practice is a visual observer standing beside you, watching the drone directly and the sky, in constant verbal contact. Solo BVLOS (beyond visual line of sight) requires a specific FAA waiver and is not a casual option.

Other operating rules to internalize

  • Do not fly over people who are not participating in the operation (Part 107 has specific Operations Over People categories tied to the drone's weight and injury rating; don't assume you qualify).
  • One drone per pilot at a time (no simultaneous multi-aircraft without a waiver).
  • Do not fly from a moving vehicle in most cases (sparsely populated exception under Part 107).
  • Do not operate carelessly or recklessly, and never under the influence (the 8-hour "bottle to throttle" and 0.04% BAC rules apply).
  • Yield right of way to all crewed aircraft, always.
VLOS is a flight-safety rule first.
Losing sight of the aircraft means you can no longer see a helicopter, a bird, or a tower in its path. Set a personal range where you can still resolve the drone's heading, and turn back before it becomes a dot. Pair this with a tested return-to-home failsafe and a known battery reserve so a lost-link event ends with the drone coming home, not falling.

Privacy & being a good neighbor

Federal law governs the airspace, but privacy, trespass, harassment, and "peeping" are handled by state and local law and by simple decency. The fastest way to get drones banned in your town is to creep your neighbors.

  • Don't hover over or film people in their yards, pools, or through windows. "Legal altitude" is no excuse for being intrusive.
  • Ask permission before flying low over private property or events.
  • Keep distance from people and pets; a startled crowd is a safety problem.
  • If someone objects, land and talk — don't escalate. Goodwill keeps spots open.
  • Respect launch-site rules; pack out, don't block paths, keep noise reasonable.
Make a limits card.
Pros carry a small card with their own hard limits — it removes in-the-moment temptation to push altitude or range "just this once."
▸Hands-On

Write a personal operating-limits card to keep with your gear.

  1. Front: Max 400 ft AGL, VLOS at all times, VO for FPV, your personal max range.
  2. Back: privacy etiquette (no hovering over yards/windows, ask before low flights, land-and-talk if challenged).
  3. Add failsafe reminders: RTH set and tested, land at 30% battery, yield to all aircraft.
  4. Laminate or photograph it; keep a copy in your case and on your phone.

title: The DJI/NDAA Market Landscape & Insurance
html:
Why the drone you can buy is a moving target

A large share of consumer and prosumer drones are made by Chinese manufacturers, chiefly DJI (and Autel). Over several years, US policy has increasingly scrutinized foreign-made drones on national-security grounds — primarily data-security concerns (where flight logs, imagery, and telemetry could go) and supply-chain dependence. This is a genuinely evolving, politically contested area; the goal here is to explain it accurately and neutrally so you can make your own decisions, not to tell you what to buy.

The pieces of the debate

  • NDAA provisions. Various National Defense Authorization Act sections have restricted federal agencies from buying or operating certain foreign-made drones, and have driven a "Blue UAS" approved list of vetted (largely US/allied) aircraft for government and some critical-infrastructure use. These restrictions historically targeted government procurement, not consumers.
  • "Countering CCP Drones" proposals. Legislative efforts have proposed adding DJI (and sometimes others) to an FCC "covered list," which could block new equipment authorizations — meaning future models might not be legally importable or sold, even if existing units keep working. A related provision has tasked a national-security agency with reviewing DJI within a set window; if no review clears them, automatic restrictions could follow.
  • Tariffs and customs. Separately, tariff changes and customs holds have at times disrupted DJI imports and availability regardless of the security statutes.
  • State and agency bans. Some states restrict public agencies (police, fire) from using non-approved drones; rules vary widely.
Verify before you spend.
Whether a specific model can be imported, sold, or used by your category of operator changes by the month. Before buying or starting a business around a given platform, check the current FCC covered-list status, the latest NDAA/appropriations text, and the manufacturer's own statements. What is true this quarter may not be next.
Neutral takeaway.
For most recreational and small commercial flyers, foreign-made drones have generally remained legal to own and fly even as government-procurement restrictions tightened. But the trajectory points toward more scrutiny. If you're building a long-term business, weigh platform risk: consider whether a Blue UAS / US-made option fits, and don't bet a livelihood on a single import-dependent model.

Insurance

Drones crash, lose link, and occasionally hurt people or property. Insurance is optional for hobbyists and effectively mandatory for professionals.

TypeCoversWho needs it
LiabilityDamage/injury you cause to othersAnyone; required for most client work
HullDamage to your own aircraftOwners of expensive rigs
PayloadCamera/gimbal/sensor damageCinema/mapping pros
  • Hobbyist option: a recognized community-based organization membership (e.g. the AMA) typically bundles a liability policy for members flying within its safety code — an inexpensive entry point.
  • On-demand: apps like SkyWatch.AI and Thimble sell hourly or daily liability (commonly $1M coverage) you buy per job — handy for occasional paid gigs.
  • Annual commercial: dedicated UAS insurers (BWI, Avion, etc.) write year-round liability + hull, often $500–$2,000+/yr depending on coverage and aircraft value.
  • Clients and venues frequently require proof of $1M+ liability and a certificate of insurance naming them as additional insured.
No policy replaces airmanship.
Insurance pays after a crash; it doesn't prevent one. The LiPo discipline, prop checks, failsafe testing, VLOS, and pre-flight verification from this whole part are what keep you from ever filing a claim. Fly like you're uninsured even when you're not.
▸Hands-On

Summarize the market debate and price insurance for your use.

  1. Read two reputable, recent sources on the foreign-drone / NDAA situation; note the date and that it evolves.
  2. In 3–4 sentences, summarize the current state neutrally (what's restricted, for whom, what's pending).
  3. Decide your use: hobby or commercial.
  4. Get one real quote — an on-demand liability price (e.g. $1M for a day) or an AMA-style membership — and record the number.
